extracted.intended_audience: educators, public-health reformers, policymakers, and general readers interested in physical education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for creating and judging a public system of physical education (gymnastics): institutions, curricula, athletic tests, incentives, health and moral aims, and facilities. Focuses on lessons drawn from ancient Greek practice and their applicability to modern national policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular system of bodily training
rubrics_metrics.description: “With the advance of civilization and civilized modes of life, a regular system of bodily training must be substituted for the lost opportunities of physical exercise which Nature affords so abundantly to her children in the daily functions of their wild life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical education should be systematic and regular, explicitly designed to replace lost natural activity caused by civilization. The emphasis is on a sustained regimen rather than sporadic or incidental exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public provision of free training-schools, gymnasia, and race-courses
rubrics_metrics.description: “The law of Lycurgus provides free training-schools for the thorough physical education of both sexes... public authorities [should] take in hand physical education... palaestrae, gymnasia, and international race-courses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public system should include free, accessible institutions (training-schools, palaestrae, gymnasia, race-courses) funded or supported by authorities to popularize and democratize physical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of both sexes and required proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: “The law of Lycurgus provides free training-schools for the thorough physical education of both sexes, and cautions parents against giving their daughters in marriage before they had attained the prescribed degree of proficiency in certain exercises.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical education programs should be offered to both males and females; measurable proficiencies (age- or rite-based standards) are recommended as part of social expectations or readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum of gymnastics tailored to health needs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Greek physicians… had invented a special curriculum of gymnastics, which, as Aelian assures us, never failed to cure obesity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula that address specific health conditions (e.g., obesity) and include therapeutic athletic exercises prescribed by medical authorities; medical/health objectives should inform exercise selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive facilities and combined amenities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Besides the military drill-grounds and the public gymnasia... the complete apparatus for all possible sports was often combined with free baths and lecture-halls.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilities should be comprehensive: provide apparatus for varied sports, bathing facilities, and educational spaces (lecture-halls) to support physical training and its instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of amateur associations and clubs for specialized sports
rubrics_metrics.description: “The larger cities had associations for the promotion of special favorite exercises... amateur clubs, which commonly owned a race-course or a private hall.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage local clubs/associations that promote specific sports and invest in infrastructure (race-courses, halls), fostering grassroots participation and specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular public competitions and social/material incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: “Four different localities... were consecrated to the 'Panhellenic games'... The victors... were exempt from taxation, became the idols of their native towns, were secured against the vicissitudes of fortune... and enjoyed... a liberally-endowed annuity fund.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize periodic competitions (local to national) and attach clear social and material rewards (honor, financial security, exemptions) to motivate participation and excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete physical standards/tests for recruitment and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: “The gymnastic tests... would appear...: jump their own height vertically, and thrice their own length horizontally, and two-thirds of those distances in full armor; pitch a weight equal to one-third of their own to a distance of twenty yards, and throw a javelin with such dexterity that they would not miss a mark of the size of a man's head more than four out of ten times at a distance of fifty yards...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt measurable, specific physical tests (vertical/horizontal jumps, weight pitching distance, javelin accuracy, weapons skills) as objective selection or proficiency criteria. The passage provides explicit numeric thresholds and accuracy rates as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of athletic training as preventive and therapeutic for bodily and mental health
rubrics_metrics.description: “Physical exercise, by accelerating the circulation of the blood, stimulates the activity of all those internal organs... and counteracts innumerable functional disorders... Mental pathology, if rightly understood, is a physiological science which must recognize the intimate connection and interaction of soul and body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate programs by health outcomes: improved organ function, reduction of functional disorders, and positive effects on mental health. Treat physical education as both preventive medicine and therapeutic intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of healthy outlets to reduce vice and social ills
rubrics_metrics.description: “Athletic exercises have a moral value... they afford a diversion and a vent to those animal energies which otherwise are sure to explode in debauch and all kind of vicious excesses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs to channel energy into constructive athletic pursuits as a social strategy to reduce alcohol abuse, opiate use, and other vices; measure success by reduced incidence of such behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on outdoor labor/exercise but recognition that exercise (even indoors) matters more than mere exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: “Open-air labor is the most effective cosmetic... But the remedial virtue of labor, i.e., sound bodily exercise, is greater than that of open-air life per se... we frequently find models of health and vigor [among those] who perform a large portion of their hard work in-doors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote outdoor work and exercise for aesthetic and health benefits, but prioritize the quality and intensity of bodily exercise itself; indoor programs can be equally effective if they provide substantive physical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural recognition and honors for athletic achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: “If any athlete received more than one prize... his victory was commemorated by a statue executed by the best contemporary sculptor of his native state... these statues were erected in the shade of majestic trees...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize cultural honors (statues, public recognition, festivals) to raise the prestige of athletic achievement and integrate it into civic life as an incentive mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure success by population-level health and longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The second census of Trajan furnishes some curious statistics... among the 28,000,000 inhabitants... there were 11,000 centenarians... the proportion of centenarians... was considerably lower [in other regions].”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic and epidemiological metrics (rates of centenarians, longevity distributions, incidence of chronic disease) as long-term indicators of the effectiveness of national physical-education policies.
